title: Revisiting the Upper Bild of Quaternionic Numerical Ranges

paper.title: Revisiting the Upper Bild of Quaternionic Numerical Ranges
paper.abstract:
Abstract The upper bild of the quaternionic numerical range provides a convex representative of the generally nonconvex quaternionic numerical range. Although its convexity is known, the geometry of the upper bild is difficult to describe explicitly, even for 2 × 2 2\times 2 quaternionic matrices. In this paper, we revisit the upper bild of quaternionic numerical ranges from both algebraic and geometric viewpoints. We first point out gaps in Kumar’s proof. We then investigate several special classes of 2 × 2 2\times 2 quaternionic matrices and describe their shapes and boundary
structures in the closed upper complex half-plane directly in
terms of the standard eigenvalues and the off-diagonal entry
of the Schur form. For the general 2 × 2 2\times 2 case, we use a different canonical form.
Following So and Thompson, we prove the concavity of the upper-boundary
function through the associated complex representation.
For the lower boundary, we obtain a distance-to-a-disk representation
and use convex optimization to prove its convexity.
We also treat the degenerate cases.
Together with the connectedness of the vertical sections, these
results give an alternative proof of the convexity of the upper
bild for arbitrary quaternionic matrices.

sections.text:
The numerical range is a classical object in matrix analysis and operator theory that encodes spectral and geometric information about a matrix. For a complex matrix, the celebrated Toeplitz–Hausdorff theorem asserts that the numerical range is always a convex subset of the complex plane. In contrast, the numerical range of a quaternionic matrix need not be convex. Nevertheless, the upper bild of the quaternionic numerical range is always convex So and Thompson (1996) . Although the quaternionic numerical range enjoys several algebraic properties such as Minkowski-type inclusion, unitary invariance, and affine equivariance, the upper bild should be regarded as a nonlinear orbit representative rather than a linear projection. In general, taking the upper bild of the numerical range of a quaternionic matrix does not commute with algebraic operations on matrices. So and Thompson (1996) established the convexity of bild + ⁡ ( A ) \operatorname{bild}^{+}(A) . Their proof first reduces the general n × n n	imes n case to the 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case. They then divide the 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case into several special cases and one generic case, and study them separately using explicit parametrizations and detailed calculations. For the upper boundary, So and Thompson used a result implicit in Kippenhahn (1951) , which states that the upper boundary of the bild coincides with the upper boundary of the complex numerical range of its complex representation. Since the latter is convex by the Toeplitz–Hausdorff theorem, its upper boundary function is concave. In the generic 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case, the lower boundary is divided into three parts: a left nonreal branch, a line segment on the real axis, and a right nonreal branch. They proved that the derivative of the lower boundary function is monotonically increasing on each of the two nonreal branches. Since the lower boundary function is nonnegative and vanishes on the middle real-axis interval, the three parts fit together to form a convex lower boundary function. Together with the concavity of the upper boundary function and the connectedness of the vertical sections, this proves the convexity of the upper bild in the generic 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case. The special 2 × 2 2	imes 2 cases are treated separately. Combining these special cases with the generic case proves the convexity of the upper bild for every 2 × 2 2	imes 2 quaternionic matrix. Finally, by the reduction from the general n × n n	imes n case to the 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case, the convexity of the upper bild follows for every quaternionic matrix. Kumar (2019) later claimed to give a new proof of the convexity of the upper bild. However, there are several gaps in the proof. We explain them in Section 2 . Recently, Carvalho (2026) gave an independent proof of the convexity of the upper bild. His proof introduces real coordinates on a sphere and extends two representations of the upper bild to the closed unit ball without changing their images. The two radius functions agree on the sphere, while their extensions to the ball are convex and concave, respectively. Minimizing the convex function and maximizing the concave function over affine fibres with a fixed real part yield a convex lower boundary and a concave upper boundary. This gives a concise and conceptual proof of the convexity of the upper bild. In this paper, we study the geometry of the upper bild for several special classes of 2 × 2 2	imes 2 quaternionic matrices and give an alternative proof of its convexity for arbitrary quaternionic matrices. We also begin by reducing the general n × n n	imes n problem to the 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case. We also use a quotient-space description of quaternionic unit vectors to remove the redundancy caused by right multiplication by unit quaternions. To study the geometry of the special classes, we use quaternionic unitary similarity to put a 2 × 2 2	imes 2 matrix in upper triangular form and reduce the number of parameters. The upper triangular form allows us to describe the geometry of these special classes in terms of the matrix parameters. As a by-product, we determine when the quaternionic numerical ranges of matrices in these classes are convex. For the general 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case, we use a different canonical form to prove the convexity of the upper bild. Following So and Thompson, we relate the upper boundary to the complex numerical range of the associated complex representation and give a detailed proof of its concavity. For the lower boundary, we use convex duality to obtain a distance-to-a-disk representation in a fixed positive-definite quadratic metric and prove that the lower-boundary function is convex. Degenerate cases are treated directly or by approximation. Together with the connectedness of the vertical sections, these results establish the convexity of the upper bild for every 2 × 2 2	imes 2 quaternionic matrix, and hence in every dimension. This distance-based argument differs from Carvalho’s sphere-to-ball construction Carvalho (2026) . The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 identifies gaps in Kumar’s proof. Section 3 reduces the general problem to the 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case and introduces the quotient-space framework used throughout the paper. Section 4 studies several special classes of 2 × 2 2	imes 2 quaternionic matrices. Section 5 treats the general 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case and completes the proof of the convexity of the upper bild. Finally, Section 6 summarizes the main results and discusses possible directions for future research.

sections.text: In this section, we first show that the upper boundary of the upper bild of an n × n n\times n quaternionic matrix is concave. We then consider the generic 2 × 2 2\times 2 case and prove that the lower-boundary function is convex by expressing it as the distance from an affinely moving point to a disk with concave radius. Together with Lemma 9 , these boundary properties imply the convexity of the upper bild in the 2 × 2 2\times 2 case. Lemma 6 then extends the result to arbitrary dimension. The following fact is implicit in Kippenhahn (1951) ; Kippenhahn (2008) and was later used explicitly by So and Thompson (1996) . For completeness, we provide a direct proof. Lemma 15 . sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we studied the convexity and geometry of the upper bild of the numerical range of a quaternionic matrix. For several special classes of 2 × 2 2\times 2 quaternionic matrices, we used the Schur form to obtain explicit geometric descriptions of the shape and location of the upper bild in terms of the standard eigenvalues and the off-diagonal parameters. As another application of our analysis of the special cases, we obtained some conditions for the quaternionic numerical ranges of matrices in these special classes to be convex. For the general 2 × 2 2\times 2 case, we employed a different canonical form and developed an optimization-based approach to establish the convexity of the upper bild. For the upper boundary, we related the corresponding maximization problem to the complex numerical range of the associated complex representation. We proved that the upper boundary of the upper bild coincides with that of the complex numerical range of the associated complex representation, from which the concavity of the upper-boundary function follows. For the lower boundary, we obtained a distance-to-a-disk representation and used it to prove the convexity of the lower-boundary function. Combining the concavity of the upper-boundary function, the convexity of the lower-boundary function, and the connectedness of the vertical sections, we established the convexity of the upper bild. Several questions remain open. In particular, it would be interesting to determine to what extent the algebraic and geometric properties of the upper bild of a higher-dimensional quaternionic matrix can be recovered from those of its 2 × 2 2\times 2 compressions.

sections.text: The authors thank Professor Wasin So for drawing attention to gaps in Kumar’s proof. In March 2021, he raised a question concerning Case 4 with the second author, who brought the problem to the first author’s attention in January 2025. By the time of their in-person discussion with Professor So in October 2025, the authors had identified part of the gaps discussed in this paper. The authors are grateful to Professor So for his initial observation and subsequent discussions. We also thank Professor So for drawing our attention to the question of convexity for these special classes. We became aware of the recent work of Carvalho (2026) , posted on arXiv on October 13, 2026, after completing the first draft of this manuscript. Although both papers address the convexity of the upper bild of quaternionic numerical ranges, the present paper develops a different approach based on a distance-to-a-disk formulation and provides additional results on the boundary structure. Preliminary results on the gaps in Kumar’s proof and the geometry of special classes were presented by the first author at ILAS 2026 in May 2026. The distance-to-a-disk approach was described in an abstract submitted for JMM 2027 in August 2026, before the appearance of Carvalho’s preprint.

Virginia Street, city=Reno, postcode=89557, state=Nevada, country=USA Tin-Yau Tam ttam@unr.edu https://sites.google.com/view/tinyautam/homepage Abstract The upper bild of the quaternionic numerical range provides a convex representative of the generally nonconvex quaternionic numerical range. Although its convexity is known, the geometry of the upper bild is difficult to describe explicitly, even for 2 × 2 2	imes 2 quaternionic matrices. In this paper, we revisit the upper bild of quaternionic numerical ranges from both algebraic and geometric viewpoints. We first point out gaps in Kumar’s proof. We then investigate several special classes of 2 × 2 2	imes 2 quaternionic matrices and describe their shapes and boundary structures in the closed upper complex half-plane directly in terms of the standard eigenvalues and the off-diagonal entry of the Schur form. For the general 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case, we use a different canonical form. Following So and Thompson, we prove the concavity of the upper-boundary function through the associated complex representation. For the lower boundary, we obtain a distance-to-a-disk representation and use convex optimization to prove its convexity. We also treat the degenerate cases. Together with the connectedness of the vertical sections, these results give an alternative proof of the convexity of the upper bild for arbitrary quaternionic matrices. keywords Quaternion ,Numerical range ,Convex optimization, † † credit: Conceptualization, Methodology, Formal analysis, Validation, Software, Visualization, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing † † credit: Conceptualization, Supervision, Writing – review & editing † † corresponding: Corresponding author 1 Introduction The numerical range is a classical object in matrix analysis and operator theory that encodes spectral and geometric information about a matrix. For a complex matrix, the celebrated Toeplitz–Hausdorff theorem asserts that the numerical range is always a convex subset of the complex plane. In contrast, the numerical range of a quaternionic matrix need not be convex. Nevertheless, the upper bild of the quaternionic numerical range is always convex So and Thompson (1996) . Although the quaternionic numerical range enjoys several algebraic properties such as Minkowski-type inclusion, unitary invariance, and affine equivariance, the upper bild should be regarded as a nonlinear orbit representative rather than a linear projection. In general, taking the upper bild of the numerical range of a quaternionic matrix does not commute with algebraic operations on matrices. So and Thompson (1996) established the convexity of bild + ⁡ ( A ) \operatorname{bild}^{+}(A) . Their proof first reduces the general n × n n	imes n case to the 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case. They then divide the 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case into several special cases and one generic case, and study them separately using explicit parametrizations and detailed calculations. For the upper boundary, So and Thompson used a result implicit in Kippenhahn (1951) , which states that the upper boundary of the bild coincides with the upper boundary of the complex numerical range of its complex representation. Since the latter is convex by the Toeplitz–Hausdorff theorem, its upper boundary function is concave. In the generic 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case, the lower boundary is divided into three parts: a left nonreal branch, a line segment on the real axis, and a right nonreal branch. They proved that the derivative of the lower boundary function is monotonically increasing on each of the two nonreal branches. Since the lower boundary function is nonnegative and vanishes on the middle real-axis interval, the three parts fit together to form a convex lower boundary function. Together with the concavity of the upper boundary function and the connectedness of the vertical sections, this proves the convexity of the upper bild in the generic 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case. The special 2 × 2 2	imes 2 cases are treated separately. Combining these special cases with the generic case proves the convexity of the upper bild for every 2 × 2 2	imes 2 quaternionic matrix. Finally, by the reduction from the general n × n n	imes n case to the 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case, the convexity of the upper bild follows for every quaternionic matrix. Kumar (2019) later claimed to give a new proof of the convexity of the upper bild. However, there are several gaps in the proof. We explain them in Section 2 . Recently, Carvalho (2026) gave an independent proof of the convexity of the upper bild. His proof introduces real coordinates on a sphere and extends two representations of the upper bild to the closed unit ball without changing their images. The two radius functions agree on the sphere, while their extensions to the ball are convex and concave, respectively. Minimizing the convex function and maximizing the concave function over affine fibres with a fixed real part yield a convex lower boundary and a concave upper boundary. This gives a concise and conceptual proof of the convexity of the upper bild. In this paper, we study the geometry of the upper bild for several special classes of 2 × 2 2	imes 2 quaternionic matrices and give an alternative proof of its convexity for arbitrary quaternionic matrices. We also begin by reducing the general n × n n	imes n problem to the 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case. We also use a quotient-space description of quaternionic unit vectors to remove the redundancy caused by right multiplication by unit quaternions. To study the geometry of the special classes, we use quaternionic unitary similarity to put a 2 × 2 2	imes 2 matrix in upper triangular form and reduce the number of parameters. The upper triangular form allows us to describe the geometry of these special classes in terms of the matrix parameters. As a by-product, we determine when the quaternionic numerical ranges of matrices in these classes are convex. For the general 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case, we use a different canonical form to prove the convexity of the upper bild. Following So and Thompson, we relate the upper boundary to the complex numerical range of the associated complex representation and give a detailed proof of its concavity. For the lower boundary, we use convex duality to obtain a distance-to-a-disk representation in a fixed positive-definite quadratic metric and prove that the lower-boundary function is convex. Degenerate cases are treated directly or by approximation. Together with the connectedness of the vertical sections, these results establish the convexity of the upper bild for every 2 × 2 2	imes 2 quaternionic matrix, and hence in every dimension. This distance-based argument differs from Carvalho’s sphere-to-ball construction Carvalho (2026) . The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 identifies gaps in Kumar’s proof. Section 3 reduces the general problem to the 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case and introduces the quotient-space framework used throughout the paper. Section 4 studies several special classes of 2 × 2 2	imes 2 quaternionic matrices. Section 5 treats the general 2 × 2 2	imes 2 case and completes the proof of the convexity of the upper bild. Finally, Section 6 summarizes the main results and discusses possible directions for future research. 2 Gaps in Kumar’s paper In this section, we use the notation W ℍ + ​ ( A ) W_{\mathbb{H}}^{+}(A) from Kumar (2019) ; in our notation, this set is bild + ⁡ ( A ) \operatorname{bild}^{+}(A) .
